challenges.claim: pmarks_2Chr.json places SAMEKH after both 2Chr.28.11 and 2Chr.28.13, interior to this span, neither mentioned alongside the cited 28:15 PE. Three mark breaks across seven verses again means the boundary-adjacent PE carries less distinguishing weight than its solo citation implies.
challenges.suggested_action: Disclose the 28:11/28:13 SAMEKH breaks next to the 28:15 PE citation, or note that mark density through this stretch is not diagnostic rather than presenting one mark as if it stood alone.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the strongest of the eight repairs. The concession is real, the envelope argument is checkable, and it checks: v12 brings on four men named for the first time, v15 resumes them anaphorically as the men designated by name without adding a party, and both verses carry the same verb form. Mark data matches (SAMEKH at 28:11 and 28:13 interior, PE at 28:15 on the close), and Samaria does bracket the scene at v8 and v15 as the closing caveat says. One number does not survive the check: six is the count of the bare verb across the book, not of the verb-plus-named-group construction the sentence attributes to it.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative calls v12's device “the same vayyaqumu-plus-named-group construction this book uses six times (20:19, 28:12, 28:15, 29:12, 30:14, 30:27)”. Six is right for the verb and wrong for the construction: my own consonantal sweep returns exactly those six verses for the plural verb, but 30:14 reads “וַיָּקֻ֕מוּ וַיָּסִ֨ירוּ֙” with no group expressed at all, 20:19 (“וַיָּקֻ֧מוּ הַלְוִיִּ֛ם”) and 30:27 (“וַיָּקֻ֜מוּ הַכֹּהֲנִ֤ים הַלְוִיִּם֙”) name only a class, and 28:15 is the anaphoric member the row itself identifies. Personal names follow the verb at 28:12 and 29:12 alone, so the construction as defined stands twice, not six times.
challenges.suggested_action: Separate the two counts - the plural verb stands 6x in 2Chr, the verb-plus-newly-named-persons pattern only at 28:12 and 29:12 - which sharpens rather than weakens the parallel this row draws with M8-2Chr-120.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the most sophisticated repair in the set: rather than simply retracting the 'no frame' claim, the row absorbs the challenge's own evidence and turns it into a distinction between bracketing and boundary-marking uses of the same device, then checks that distinction against a sibling decision in the same cluster instead of quietly contradicting it.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Same pattern as the row before it: each primary caught a different gap. pmarks_2Chr.json keys SAMEKH to both 28:11 and 28:13, neither mentioned beside the cited 28:15 PE, so the mark citation again understates local density without affecting the medium-confidence call it corroborates. The sharper find is OL's: 28:12's וַיָּקֻ֨מוּ אֲנָשִׁ֜ים... followed by four newly named Ephraimite leaders is a real participant-introduction frame -- the verb וַיָּקֻ֨מוּ occurs only six times in the whole book (20:19, 28:12, 28:15, 29:12, 30:14, 30:27) -- and this same cluster's own decision 120 treats the identical construction at 29:12 as the subject change that closes its span. The row's rejected_alternative asserts no frame separates 9-11 from 12-15, which this internal inconsistency contradicts. Nothing here requires moving the 9-15 span itself -- the leaders named in v12 are anaphorically the same group closing at v15, per וַיָּקֻ֣מוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים֩ אֲשֶׁר נִקְּב֨וּ בְשֵׁמ֜וֹת -- but the stated reason for keeping them together needs re-grounding, and the row's own admission of debatable edges already anticipated this stretch would not close cleanly.

challenge_responses.response: Accepted. pmarks_2Chr.json places SAMEKH after both 28:11 and 28:13, interior to the span, neither disclosed alongside the cited 28:15 PE. Disclosed both. Added oshb refs for 28:11 (SAMEKH, single-witness) and 28:13.

Accepted. v12's vayyaqumu-plus-named-leaders clause is a genuine participant-change frame this same cluster treats as boundary-closing at 29:12 (decision 120) -- the 'no frame reopening' claim was internally inconsistent. Rewrote strongest_rejected_alternative: the construction recurs at v15 anaphorically (same four leaders, same verb), so it brackets one scene rather than opening a second one here, unlike its stand-alone use at 29:12. Span 28:9-28:15 is unaffected; added oshb refs for 28:12, 28:15, 29:12, 20:19, 30:14, 30:27.
Rev round: peer ruling supported; remedy applied in micro round r2 (see rev_peer.json and final_rows_edits.json entry for M8-2Chr-115).

boss_ruling.reasoning: The no-frame claim is contradicted by the named-men frame this cluster elsewhere treats as boundary-marking; the amendment concedes the frame and defends inclusion via the anaphoric closure, rival preserved.

post_resolution_check.notes: The plural-verb-plus-newly-named-persons construction is checked against all six book-wide occurrences of the form (20:19, 28:12, 28:15, 29:12, 30:14, 30:27), and the narrower two-instance pattern the row isolates (v.12 and 29:12) holds up against the full list.

primary_reviews.rationale: Opening evidence checks out. The 28:16 and 28:20 slices are byte-exact, the parenthetical renderings match WEB word for word ('At that time King Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria', 'gave him trouble, but didn't strengthen him'), and the temporal frame is a genuine 2Chr device: בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא occurs eight times (7:8, 13:18, 16:7 with prefixed waw, 16:10, 21:10, 28:16, 30:3, 35:17), and at 16:7 it opens a prophet episode in exactly the unit-initial way this row needs — וּבָעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא בָּ֚א חֲנָ֣נִי הָרֹאֶ֔ה. The closing seam is the problem: its sole warrant is a claimed echo between v22 and v16, and at root level the Hebrew ties v22 backwards into this very span instead.

challenges.claim: The 21/22 seam is carried entirely by the assertion that v22 'echoes v16's own wording'. In the Hebrew the shared material is only the noun for 'time' with its prefixed preposition; the distinctive element of וּבְעֵת֙ הָצֵ֣ר ל֔וֹ is a verbatim pickup of v20's וַיָּ֥צַר ל֖וֹ — same root, same prepositional object, two verses earlier and inside this row — and the pairing is a fixed 2Chr idiom, recurring at 33:12 as וּכְהָצֵ֣ר ל֔וֹ. Read from the text, v22 is anaphoric to the last narrative event of the span it is supposed to be distinguished from, which is cohesion across the proposed seam rather than a matching frame at it. Meanwhile the one distinctive seam signal at v22 goes uncited: the resumptive full naming ה֖וּא הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אָחָֽז, a sequence that occurs nowhere else in 2Chr.
challenges.suggested_action: Re-ground the close on the unique resumptive-naming clause that ends v22, and describe the distress phrase as an anaphor of v20 rather than an echo of v16; if the echo argument is kept as the primary warrant, the medium confidence should come down, since it currently rests on the weaker of the two available readings.

primary_reviews.rationale: The paired 'time' frames at v16 and v22 (בָּעֵת הַהִיא / וּבְעֵת הָצֵר לוֹ) are a genuinely strong echo device and both quotes check out byte-exact against oshb -- this is one of the cluster's better-argued seams. The v20 closing quote is likewise exact. A translation-fidelity slip turns up in how the opening quote is glossed, though.

challenges.claim: The quoted Hebrew fragment בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא שָׁלַ֞ח הַמֶּ֧לֶךְ אָחָ֛ז ends at 'Ahaz,' but the attached WEB gloss 'At that time King Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria' translates words (עַל מַלְכֵי אַשּׁוּר לַעְזֹר לוֹ) that are not part of the quoted span, with no ellipsis marking the extension. The same row's other translator glosses stay within their quote's coverage.
challenges.suggested_action: Either lengthen the Hebrew quote to include עַל מַלְכֵי אַשּׁוּר לַעְזֹר לוֹ, or trim the gloss to 'At that time King Ahaz sent...' with an ellipsis showing the cut.

primary_reviews.rationale: The re-grounding is sound and its central factual claim verifies: a consonantal sweep for the hu-hammelekh sequence returns 28:22 and nothing else in the book, so calling that resumptive naming unattested elsewhere is exact, and the distress idiom does recur at 33:12 independently of this pairing. The v16 quotation and its gloss now match WEB word for word. The remaining defect sits at the other end of the span, where the row's one-clause characterization of its own final verse misstates both who acts in it and what is new in it.

challenges.claim: The rationale ends the span “with v21 restating the plundered tribute”. Neither half fits 28:21, which reads “כִּֽי חָלַ֤ק אָחָז֙” ... “וַיִּתֵּן֙ לְמֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר”: Ahaz is the agent, apportioning from temple, palace and officials and handing it over, so this is a payment made rather than plunder taken from him, and nothing in vv16-20 states it earlier, so it restates nothing. The plunder of this chapter (28:8) belongs to the Israelite army and to a different row.
challenges.suggested_action: Describe v21 as the Hebrew has it - Ahaz stripping temple and palace treasuries to pay Assyria, with the closing wela le-ezra lo sealing the failure already stated in v20 - instead of as a restated tribute.

primary_reviews.rationale: The row also strengthens its own case beyond the original complaint: the v22 idiom comparison to 33:12 and the 'nowhere else' claim about the resumptive full-title naming both check out against the text, so the fix isn't just a quote-length patch but sits inside an argument that survives its own added scrutiny.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Two independent problems, neither touching the row's Hebrew quotations, which all check out. LF is right that the parenthetical gloss attached to the opening quote runs past what the Hebrew actually covers: the cited fragment בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא שָׁלַ֞ח הַמֶּ֧לֶךְ אָחָ֛ז stops at 'Ahaz,' but 28:16's remainder, עַל מַלְכֵ֥י אַשּׁ֖וּר לַעְזֹ֥ר לֽוֹ ('to the kings of Assyria to help him'), is folded into the translation with no ellipsis marking the cut. OL's find is more consequential for the row's own argument: v22's וּבְעֵת֙ הָצֵ֣ר ל֔וֹ shares only the bare noun 'time' with v16, but reproduces v20's וַיָּ֥צַר ל֖וֹ root-for-root and suffix-for-suffix -- an anaphor pulling v22 backward into the very span the row wants it kept apart from, not an echo of the row's own opening frame. A consonantal sweep confirms the alternative seam-signal OL proposes instead is real and unique: הוא המלך in that exact sequence appears nowhere else in 2Chr but at v22's close. Neither finding requires re-drawing the 16-21 boundary on its own; both bear on how much weight the medium confidence should place on the 'matching echo' warrant, which the author round should weigh.

challenge_responses.response: Accepted. The quoted Hebrew fragment stopped at 'Ahaz,' but the attached gloss ran partway into the verse's remainder ('to the kings of Assyria') without an ellipsis and without reaching the verse's actual end ('to help him'). Extended the Hebrew quote to the full verse and completed the gloss to match it exactly, curing both the cut and the partial-coverage mismatch.

Accepted. v22's distress-clause shares only the bare noun 'time' with v16, but reproduces v20's verb root-for-root and suffix-for-suffix -- an anaphor pulling v22 backward into the span it's supposed to be distinguished from, and the idiom recurs independently at 33:12, so it isn't even unique to this pairing. Re-grounded the close on the real, previously-uncited signal: v22's resumptive full-title naming, unattested elsewhere in the book. Since the seam now rests on this stronger clause rather than the discredited echo, medium confidence is kept rather than lowered -- the peer's caution about lowering applied only if the weak reading were retained. Added oshb/web refs for 28:20 and oshb/web for 33:12.
Rev round: peer ruling supported; remedy applied in micro round r2 (see rev_peer.json and final_rows_edits.json entry for M8-2Chr-116).

boss_ruling.reasoning: The echo picks up v20, not v16, and the unique royal-naming clause was the uncited signal; re-anchored accordingly.

post_resolution_check.notes: A direct search turns up the full-title resumptive naming 'this same King Ahaz' at v.22 alone, nowhere else across all thirty-six chapters, so the row's uniqueness claim for the real seam-signal is exact rather than asserted.

primary_reviews.rationale: All three quoted runs are byte-exact and the summary matches the verses: sacrifice to the Damascus gods at v23, the cutting up of temple vessels at v24 (וַיְקַצֵּץ֙ אֶת כְּלֵ֣י בֵית הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים), high places in every city at v25. The close is the securest edge in this cluster after 28:27 — v26 opens with the tier-1 source-citation formula וְיֶ֤תֶר דְּבָרָיו֙, whose heading word stands at exactly ten reign-closures in 2Chr (13:22, 20:34, 25:26, 26:22, 27:7, 28:26, 32:32, 33:18, 35:26, 36:8). I also tested the rejected alternative's 'no intervening scene-change marker' wording and found it sound: v24 does re-name the king, וַיֶּאֱסֹ֨ף אָחָ֜ז, but that re-nomination follows the direct speech quoted in v23 and is default participant tracking in Hebrew narrative, not a segmentation signal. One piece of in-book support the row does not claim and could: v24's וַיִּסְגֹּ֖ר אֶת דַּלְת֣וֹת בֵּית יְהוָ֑ה is answered antithetically at 29:3 by פָּתַ֛ח אֶת דַּלְת֥וֹת בֵּית יְהוָ֖ה and recalled inside Hezekiah's own speech at 29:7 as סָֽגְר֞וּ דַּלְת֣וֹת הָאוּלָ֗ם — an in-book link of the kind the strategy admits as literary evidence, and it argues for keeping the door-closing inside the Ahaz apostasy row. The row's opening 'matching echo' wording shares the weakness I document under M8-2Chr-116; that is one seam, adjudicated once, and I do not re-file it here.

The 'time of his distress' opening properly answers v16's paired frame, and the closing high-places-in-every-city line is byte-exact against oshb, with v26's source-citation formula genuinely starting fresh material the next verse. The one plausible internal split -- v24's re-named subject ('Ahaz gathered...') resuming narrative action right after the quoted Damascus-gods speech in v23 -- is not actually a distinct seam once compared against how the cluster treats an identical pattern elsewhere: v14 also resumes narrative action ('the armed men left...') with a freshly-named subject straight after quoted speech (the Ephraimite leaders' answer closing at v13), and that row keeps it as continuation, not a boundary. Applying the same standard here, this row's merge is consistent rather than special-pleaded.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Neither primary challenged this row, and a spot-check of its three quoted runs (28:22-23 Damascus-gods material, 28:24's temple-vessel cutting, 28:25's every-city high places) against oshb finds them byte-exact, with 28:26's source-citation formula genuinely opening fresh material as claimed. The rejected_alternative's account of v23-24 as continuous participant-tracking (a renamed subject after quoted speech, not a scene break) also holds against the identical pattern this cluster's own decision 115 exhibits at 28:13-14, so the merge is argued consistently rather than special-pleaded.

post_resolution_check.notes: The matched 'time' echo between v.16's opener and v.22's distress clause collates against oshb, and the escalating trespass catalog running through v.25 is coherent as a single unbroken movement.

primary_reviews.rationale: The two long quotations (28:26 entire, 28:27 entire) are byte-exact, the PE cite is right — pmarks keys PE to 2Chr.28.27 — and the count is right too: this is the fourth source-citation closure in the 25:1-28:27 stretch, all four headed by the same formula word (25:26, 26:22, 27:7, 28:26). The row's reading of the burial clause as grammatically inseparable from the death formula is likewise borne out, since the causal clause כִּ֚י לֹ֣א הֱבִיאֻ֔הוּ לְקִבְרֵ֖י מַלְכֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל depends on the preceding wayyiqtol pair and cannot stand alone. Two comparative claims in the rationale, however, are contradicted by the verses they name.

challenges.claim: The register is misattributed to Uzziah. 26:22 names no book of kings at all: וְיֶ֨תֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י עֻזִּיָּ֔הוּ הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאֲחֲרֹנִ֑ים כָּתַ֛ב יְשַֽׁעְיָ֥הוּ בֶן אָמ֖וֹץ הַנָּבִֽיא — the source is a prophet's writing (WEB: 'Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, wrote'). Sweeping the register phrase across 2Chr returns seven verses — 20:34, 25:26, 27:7, 28:26, 32:32, 35:27, 36:8 — and 26:22 is not among them. Within this part the dual-kingdom register is named for Amaziah, עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵי יְהוּדָ֖ה וְיִשְׂרָאֵֽל, for Jotham, עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִיהוּדָֽה, and now for Ahaz; and Jotham's inverts the order of the two kingdoms relative to Ahaz's, which is a detail worth having right in a row whose argument is that the same register recurs.
challenges.suggested_action: Replace Uzziah with Jotham in the comparandum list, note the inverted kingdom order at 27:7, and either drop 26:22 or describe it for what it is — a prophet-authorship citation rather than a register citation. Mirror 26:22 and 27:7 into boundary_evidence_refs if they remain argued.

challenges.claim: 'An exclusion notice unique to Ahaz among this part's kings' overstates what the part contains. 26:23 gives Uzziah the same formal shape — differentiated burial followed by a causal clause supplying the reason: וַיִּקְבְּר֨וּ אֹת֤וֹ עִם אֲבֹתָיו֙ בִּשְׂדֵ֤ה הַקְּבוּרָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לַמְּלָכִ֔ים כִּ֥י אָמְר֖וּ מְצוֹרָ֣ע ה֑וּא. Against that, 28:27 reads כִּ֚י לֹ֣א הֱבִיאֻ֔הוּ לְקִבְרֵ֖י מַלְכֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל. Amaziah (25:28) and Jotham (27:9) do have unqualified burials, so the contrast the row wants exists; it is a two-member pattern in this part, not a unique feature of Ahaz.
challenges.suggested_action: Narrow the claim to what the Hebrew alone supports — Ahaz is the only one of the four said not to have been brought to the royal tombs proper, לְקִבְרֵ֖י — and cite 26:23 as the in-part comparandum instead of implying no parallel exists.

primary_reviews.rationale: The core boundary evidence is solid: the source-citation and death-and-succession formulas both quote byte-exact against 28:26-27, and the PE mark cited at v27 matches pmarks_2Chr.json precisely. The row's two comparative claims about how this closing pattern relates to the part's other three kings don't survive a check against their actual verses, however, and both need correcting.

challenges.claim: 2Chr.26.22 reads וְיֶ֨תֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י עֻזִּיָּ֔הוּ הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאֲחֲרֹנִ֑ים כָּתַ֛ב יְשַֽׁעְיָ֥הוּ בֶן אָמ֖וֹץ הַנָּבִֽיא -- 'Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, wrote' (WEB) -- a prophetic-authorship citation, not a reference to 'the book of the kings of Judah and Israel' the way 25:26 (Amaziah) and 28:26 (Ahaz) actually read. The row's claim that the formula here 'again point[s] to the dual-kingdom register named for Amaziah, Uzziah, and now Ahaz' misdescribes Uzziah's verse, which is a different citation device entirely.
challenges.suggested_action: Remove Uzziah from the dual-kingdom-register grouping, or note explicitly that his source-citation is the prophetic-authorship variant rather than the register variant that Amaziah and Ahaz share.

challenges.claim: 2Chr.26.23 records Uzziah buried בִּשְׂדֵ֤ה הַקְּבוּרָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לַמְּלָכִ֔ים כִּ֥י אָמְר֖וּ מְצוֹרָ֣ע ה֑וּא -- 'in the field of burial which belonged to the kings, for they said, he is a leper' (WEB) -- a qualified, exclusionary burial notice tied to his condition, unlike the plain notices for Amaziah (25:28: buried 'with his fathers in the City of Judah') and Jotham (27:9: buried 'in David's city'). The row's claim that Ahaz's burial-exclusion clause is 'unique...among this part's kings' overlooks this Uzziah parallel.
challenges.suggested_action: Qualify 'unique' -- e.g. Ahaz's is the only one framed as an explicit non-admission (לֹא הֱבִיאֻהוּ) to the royal tombs, as distinct from Uzziah's separate-field burial, rather than claiming no other king in the part gets an exclusionary notice at all.

primary_reviews.rationale: All four cures land, and the numbers behind them are right: sweeping the construct phrase across the book returns precisely the seven verses listed, with 26:22 absent, and the kingdom order does invert at 27:7 against 25:26 and 28:26. The burial narrowing is exact as well, since leqivrei stands at 28:27 only while the book's other burial denials use a different phrase. What the repair got wrong is the name it gave the set it swept for. The dual-kingdom label fits five of the seven hits and fails at both edges of the category, which matters because this sweep is offered as the demonstration that a register exists and that Uzziah falls outside it.

challenges.claim: The rationale and the last line of boundary_evidence_refs both call the seven hits a dual-kingdom register sweep. The count is correct for the construct phrase sefer malkhei, but the category is not: 20:34 names one kingdom only, “עַל סֵ֖פֶר מַלְכֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל”, and is counted in, while 16:11, “סֵ֣פֶר הַמְּלָכִ֔ים לִיהוּדָ֖ה וְיִשְׂרָאֵֽל”, names both kingdoms in the same Judah-then-Israel order as 25:26 and 28:26 and is counted out, because it uses the article-plus-plural form with lamed rather than the construct. (24:27 is a third variant, midrash sefer ha-melakhim.) The sweep is lexical, not semantic, and the label overstates what it demonstrates.
challenges.suggested_action: Relabel the sweep as the sefer malkhei construct phrase (7 hits, 26:22 not among them), note that 20:34 inside that set names Israel alone, and either admit 16:11 as the dual-kingdom variant or state that it is excluded on form; mirror oshb:2Chr.16.11 and oshb:2Chr.20.34 into boundary_evidence_refs.

primary_reviews.rationale: All four original defects are genuinely fixed, but the replacement evidence introduces its own precision gap: the seven-verse sweep offered as proof of 'the dual-kingdom register' includes 20:34, which names only 'the kings of Israel' through Jehu's record rather than both kingdoms -- the same category error the revision was meant to correct (folding a differently-shaped citation into the register), now recurring in milder form on the count instead of on 26:22 itself.

challenges.claim: The book-wide sweep offered to correct the Uzziah misattribution overcorrects in the opposite direction. It lists 20:34 among the register phrase's seven verses alongside 25:26, 27:7, 28:26, 32:32, 35:27, and 36:8, but 20:34 reads עַל סֵָפֶר מַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, 'the book of the kings of Israel' alone, and it is itself mediated through a named individual source ('the words of Jehu the son of Hanani, which is inscribed in the book of the kings of Israel'), not the two-kingdom phrasing ('kings of Judah and Israel' or 'kings of Israel and Judah') the other six verses share. A consonantal sweep for the register phrase confirms the count of seven hits is correct, but one of the seven does not actually carry the dual-kingdom wording the sweep is offered to support, and it shares the named-source structure the row uses to disqualify 26:22 from the same register.
challenges.suggested_action: Either drop 20:34 from the seven-verse list and report six true dual-kingdom hits (25:26, 27:7, 28:26, 32:32, 35:27, 36:8), or keep the seven-verse count but flag 20:34 as the single-kingdom, named-source outlier so the sweep cannot be read as showing all seven share the two-kingdom phrasing the row's opening sentence claims for the register.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Four challenges converge on two errors, both confirmed and both worth a single combined fix rather than two. First, the register claim: 26:22 reads כָּתַ֛ב יְשַֽׁעְיָ֥הוּ בֶן אָמ֖וֹץ הַנָּבִֽיא, a prophetic-authorship citation with no 'book of the kings' phrase at all, so Uzziah does not belong beside Amaziah and Ahaz in the row's dual-kingdom-register list. LF catches the core error; OL's version is the fuller remedy, since 27:7's Jotham verse is the actual missing comparandum and it inverts the kingdom order (מַלְכֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִיהוּדָֽה, Israel-then-Judah) relative to Amaziah's and Ahaz's Judah-then-Israel phrasing -- confirmed by a book-wide sweep returning exactly seven verses carrying the register phrase (20:34, 25:26, 27:7, 28:26, 32:32, 35:27, 36:8), 26:22 not among them. One remedy: swap Jotham in for Uzziah, note the order inversion, and describe 26:22 for the different citation device it is. Second, the burial claim: 26:23 shows Uzziah also gets a differentiated, causally-explained burial (בִּשְׂדֵ֤ה הַקְּבוּרָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לַמְּלָכִ֔ים, 'because they said he is a leper'), against the plain notices for Amaziah (25:28) and Jotham (27:9), so Ahaz's exclusion is not unique in kind within the part -- both primaries converge here too, with OL's phrasing the more exact of the two: Ahaz alone is denied the royal tombs proper (לְקִבְרֵ֖י), which is narrower and true, unlike the row's flat 'unique' claim. Neither error touches the row's core boundary evidence, which is solid: the source-citation and death-succession formulas quote byte-exact, and the 28:27 PE cite matches pmarks.

challenge_responses.response: Confirmed: 26:22 reads כָּתַ֛ב יְשַֽׁעְיָ֥הוּ בֶן אָמ֖וֹץ הַנָּבִֽיא (WEB: "Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, wrote."), a prophetic-authorship citation with no book-of-kings phrase at all, so Uzziah does not belong beside Amaziah and Ahaz in the dual-kingdom register. Uzziah is removed from that list and replaced with Jotham (27:7).

Confirmed: 26:23 gives Uzziah a differentiated, causally-explained burial, בִּשְׂדֵ֤ה הַקְּבוּרָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לַמְּלָכִ֔ים כִּ֥י אָמְר֖וּ מְצוֹרָ֣ע ה֑וּא, against the plain notices for Amaziah (25:28) and Jotham (27:9). The claim is narrowed: Ahaz alone is denied the royal tombs proper (לְקִבְרֵ֖י), not uniquely excluded in kind.

Adopted the fuller remedy: Jotham's citation at 27:7, עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִיהוּדָֽה, replaces Uzziah as the register comparandum, its inverted kingdom order (Israel-then-Judah, against Amaziah's and Ahaz's Judah-then-Israel) is now stated, and 26:22 is described as the prophetic-authorship device it is rather than folded into the register.

Adopted the narrower phrasing this challenge proposed: Ahaz alone is said not to have been brought to the royal tombs proper (לְקִבְרֵ֖י), and 26:23 is cited as the in-part burial comparandum rather than implying no parallel exists in the part.

primary_reviews.rationale: Five quoted runs, all byte-exact, and the mark cite is correct: pmarks keys PE to 2Chr.28.27, precisely the handoff the row points at, disclosed as WLC single-witness. The 'fixed evaluation clause' label is verifiable rather than impressionistic — וַיַּ֥עַשׂ הַיָּשָׁ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה stands byte-identically at 25:2, 26:4, 29:2 and 34:2. The strongest confirmation is one the row leaves implicit: the 2/3 close is syntactic, since 29:3 steps out of the narrative wayyiqtol chain, fronting a pronoun and two date phrases before a qatal (ה֣וּא בַשָּׁנָה֩ הָרִאשׁוֹנָ֨ה לְמָלְכ֜וֹ בַּחֹ֣דֶשׁ הָרִאשׁ֗וֹן ... פָּתַ֛ח), whereas the Ahaz accession pair at 28:1 is continued by a wayyiqtol (וַיֵּ֕לֶךְ). That single contrast is exactly why this cluster can isolate 29:1-2 and could not isolate 28:1-2, so rows M8-2Chr-113 and M8-2Chr-119 are consistent on Hebrew grounds rather than by preference. Two observations that do not disturb the row: 29:1's age notice has its own word order, יְחִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ מָלַ֗ךְ בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֤ים וְחָמֵשׁ֙ שָׁנָ֔ה, unlike the pattern at 25:1, 26:3, 27:1 and 28:1 (בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֤ים שָׁנָה֙ אָחָ֣ז בְּמָלְכ֔וֹ), and it carries a maternal-name element, וְשֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔וֹ אֲבִיָּ֖ה בַּת זְכַרְיָֽהוּ, that the Ahaz notice lacks — both reinforce, if anything, its status as a self-contained regnal notice.

Every Hebrew fragment quoted -- the death-and-succession handoff, the age-formula halves, and the evaluation clause -- lines up byte-exact against oshb 28:27 and 29:1-2, and the PE mark cited at the 28:27/29:1 seam matches pmarks_2Chr.json, consistent with decision 118's own citation of the same mark from the other side. primary_reviews.rationale: Four quoted runs collate exactly and the mark is right — pmarks keys SAMEKH to 2Chr.29.11, correctly disclosed as single-witness — as are the two junctions the row does argue. At 4/5 the inset rule genuinely applies: v4 ends on לִרְח֥וֹב הַמִּזְרָֽח and v5 opens וַיֹּ֥אמֶר לָהֶ֖ם with nothing intervening, so no resumption frame isolates the charge speech. The gap is the junction the row crosses without argument, between the dated first-act notice and the summons that follows it.

challenges.claim: A tier-1 device sits unargued inside this nine-verse span. 29:4 is a gathering frame in full form — וַיָּבֵ֥א אֶת הַכֹּהֲנִ֖ים וְאֶת הַלְוִיִּ֑ם וַיַּֽאַסְפֵ֖ם לִרְח֥וֹב הַמִּזְרָֽח — functionally the same summons device as 15:9 (וַיִּקְבֹּ֗ץ), 20:4 (וַיִּקָּבְצ֣וּ), 23:2 (וַיִּקְבְּצ֤וּ) and 34:29 (וַיֶּאֱסֹ֕ף); note in passing that the summons verbs here are of the gathering roots rather than the qahal family the strategy's §1 label implies. The Hebrew also makes the preceding verse formally detachable: 29:3 sits off the wayyiqtol backbone altogether, putting an independent pronoun and two date phrases ahead of a qatal, פָּתַ֛ח, with only the suffixed וַֽיְחַזְּקֵֽם attached, whereas the chain proper starts at v4 with וַיָּבֵ֥א. The row argues 4-to-5 and 11-to-12 but never the 3/4 junction it crosses, and at ~4.8 verses per decision across this draft a nine-verse merge over an unargued tier-1 frame is exactly the case the granularity rule asks to be justified.
challenges.suggested_action: Argue the 3/4 junction explicitly — either that v3 is a dated heading governing the summons and the charge that follow, in which case say so and cite the fronted pronoun construction, or that it is a self-standing first-act notice and the row should open at v4. If the summons frame is cited in support, name its verb correctly rather than by the qahal-family label.

primary_reviews.rationale: The dated first-year/first-month notice opening the row and the SAMEKH mark after v11 both check out against oshb and pmarks_2Chr.json respectively. Considered whether v12's turn to a multi-clan Levite roster (Kohathites, Merarites, Gershonites, and more) is a stronger resumption-frame than the row credits, since it reads as a genuine list/register-formula shift rather than plain narrative continuation -- but the row's actual rejected_alternative only concerns whether 29:5-11 should detach from its own introduction in 29:3-4, not whether the span should run past v11, so this observation reinforces rather than undercuts the close the row already argues from the subject-shift and the mark.

The junction the challenge asked about is argued now, and the syntactic description of v3 checks out against the text: independent pronoun, two date phrases, qatal, then one suffixed wayyiqtol, with the chain proper resuming at v4. The three WEB renderings quoted at 29:3, 29:5 and 29:11 are verbatim, and the SAMEKH after v11 is correctly marked single-witness. But the two fields now say opposite things about v3. The rationale treats it as the dated first act from which the summons follows; the rejected alternative denies it any action of its own and reduces it to a date phrase, and that is what the merge argument then rests on.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative states that “v3 supplies no independent action of its own apart from the summons it introduces” and that isolating it would “strand a date phrase”. The verse carries two finite verbs with Hezekiah as subject and the temple doors as object, “פָּתַ֛ח אֶת דַּלְת֥וֹת בֵּית יְהוָ֖ה וַֽיְחַזְּקֵֽם”, and the row's own rationale quotes it as a dated act, calls the 3/4 join one continuous first-act notice, and glosses the WEB as the opening and repair of those doors. The two fields cannot both be right, and the merge warrant is carried by the one the Hebrew contradicts.
challenges.suggested_action: Re-argue the merge on sequence rather than emptiness - v3 is a complete dated first act whose immediate consequence is the summons of v4, with no frame intervening - and drop both the claim that v3 has no action and the description of it as a stranded date phrase. (The row's reference to the rival that this challenge raised is covered separately under ROL-M8-2Chr-114-1.)

primary_reviews.rationale: Collation is clean: the row's six Hebrew runs (29:12, 29:15 twice, 29:17, 29:18, 29:19) each reproduce the pointed text byte for byte and each resolves to exactly the verse it is credited to. Mark typing is right as well — pmarks_2Chr.json keys SAMEKH to 29:11 and SAMEKH to 29:19, both WLC single-witness, neither being one of the book's two double-mark verses — and both are used as corroboration behind textual signals rather than as drivers. Chapter 29 lies in the identical-numbering stretch of the crosswalk (WEB 15:1-36:23 = MT), so no dual-cite is owed and none is offered; that arithmetic is correct. What the Hebrew will not underwrite is the row's silence about 29:18. There the wayyiqtol opens with a movement plus a change of addressee — וַיָּב֤וֹאוּ פְנִ֨ימָה֙ אֶל חִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ — and a first-person-plural report then runs unbroken to the end of 29:19 (טִהַ֖רְנוּ … הֵכַ֣נּוּ וְהִקְדָּ֑שְׁנוּ), with the tier-3 SAMEKH sitting at 29:17 immediately before it. The row quotes that speech but never says why it stays inside an eight-verse span. Disclosure the row also omits: pmarks records SAMEKH keyed to 29:13, 29:14 and 29:17 inside the span, so its edge-only mark citation is selective (marks are never counterevidence by absence, and I press none of them as a driver). Cohesion evidence exists on the other side and is likewise unused: פנימה occurs in 2Chr only at 3:4, 29:16 and 29:18, so וַיָּבֹ֣אוּ הַ֠כֹּהֲנִים לִפְנִ֣ימָה בֵית יְהוָה֮ לְטַהֵר֒ and the 29:18 clause form a lexical pair binding the unit. Finally the type label credits the cleansing to the Levites, while 29:16 gives the inner-house purge to the priests and leaves the Levites the relay: וַֽיְקַבְּלוּ֙ הַלְוִיִּ֔ם לְהוֹצִ֥יא לְנַֽחַל קִדְר֖וֹן חֽוּצָה.

challenges.claim: Tier-1 seam inside the span goes unargued. 29:18 begins וַיָּב֤וֹאוּ פְנִ֨ימָה֙ אֶל חִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ (WEB 'Then they went in to Hezekiah the king within the palace and said'): a location change, a new addressee, and a direct-speech frame whose 1cp verbs (טִהַ֖רְנוּ … הֵכַ֣נּוּ וְהִקְדָּ֑שְׁנוּ) carry to the end of 29:19, with a tier-3 single-witness SAMEKH at 29:17 abutting it. The row quotes the speech as content but never addresses whether 29:18-19 is a report unit in its own right; its rejected alternative tests only the 29:20 edge.
challenges.suggested_action: Argue the 29:18 seam explicitly in the rationale or rejected_alternative — the פנימה echo between 29:16 and 29:18 (the only two occurrences in the reign, 3:4 aside) is the natural cohesion answer — or split 29:12-17 / 29:18-19.

The Levites open the span at 29:12 and are the roll of 12-14, but the purge of the inner house is priestly.

primary_reviews.rationale: The subject-change opening (Levites arising right after the SAMEKH-marked close of Hezekiah's speech) and the dated-completion/report closing both stand up as genuine tier-1 seams, and the rejected alternative correctly names 29:20's new-day, new-actor shift as the true rival rather than a straw option.

challenges.claim: The 29:15 fragment is rendered 'וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ כְמִצְוַת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ בְּדִבְרֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה ... לְטַהֵ֖ר בֵּ֥ית יְהוָֽה,' but 2Chr_oshb.txt's 2Chr.29.15 line reads '...וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ כְמִצְוַת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ בְּדִבְרֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה לְטַהֵ֖ר בֵּ֥ית יְהוָֽה' with יְהוָ֑ה and לְטַהֵ֖ר directly adjacent -- the ellipsis marks an elision that is not present in the source.
challenges.suggested_action: Remove the ellipsis so the citation reads as one continuous MT clause, or replace it with whatever intervening words were actually intended.

primary_reviews.rationale: All three obligations were met on their face — the false break at 29:15 is gone, the type label names priestly agency, and the 29:17|18 seam is finally defended — but the defence rests on a grammatical claim that collation will not support. Citation hygiene is otherwise sound here: six Hebrew runs are byte-exact against oshb and six WEB slices are verbatim, so the trouble is categorisation, not drift. The item shared by 29:16 and 29:18 is פנימה, an adverbial locative, and the row calls it a rare verb-root that named an entry; the underlying sweep is correct (3:4, 29:16, 29:18, nothing else in the book), which is why a relabel rather than a retraction is what is owed. A second, independent problem: the row's use of tier-3 marks runs one way only, citing the SAMEKHs at its two edges as support while leaving the SAMEKH after 29:17 — sitting on the very seam under dispute — and those after 29:13 and 29:14 unmentioned. The sweep note has also been parked inside the refs array.

challenges.claim: The cohesion argument across 29:17|18 turns on "the same rare verb-root that named the priests' own entry to the inner house at 29:16 -- occurring only at 3:4 and these two verses in the whole book", and no such verb exists. Read as intended, the shared item is פנימה (לִפְנִ֣ימָה at 29:16, פְנִ֨ימָה֙ at 29:18, מִפְּנִ֖ימָה at 3:4): an adverbial locative built on the noun פנים, not a verb, and at 3:4 it stands in וַיְצַפֵּ֥הוּ מִפְּנִ֖ימָה זָהָ֥ב טָהֽוֹר, where nobody enters anything, so it names no entry there. Read the other way, the shared item is the actual verb of entry, בוא, whose 3mp wayyiqtol alone stands sixteen times in the book (ויבאו at 5:4, 8:18, 15:12, 18:29, 20:2, 20:28, 23:2, 23:17, 23:20, 24:23, 29:15, 29:16, 30:11, 31:8, 34:9, plus plene ויבואו once at 29:18), which destroys the exclusivity claim outright and also puts that verb at 29:15 (וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ), a verse the row quotes without counting. Either way the sentence misdescribes the form its near-far argument depends on, and the row's WEB slice for 29:18 stops just before "within the palace", which hides that the two interiors differ: the temple's inner house at 29:16 against the king's presence at 29:18.
challenges.suggested_action: Recast the echo as an adverbial-locative lexeme sweep (פנימה at 3:4, 29:16 and 29:18, three attestations, independently reproduced), strike "rare verb" and "verb-root" from both the rationale and the rejected alternative, and say what the difference in referent does to the inference that execution and report form one movement.

challenges.claim: Tier-3 corroboration is applied in one direction. The row annotates the SAMEKHs following 29:11 and 29:19 as support for its two edges, but lists oshb:2Chr.29.17 with no mark annotation although pmarks_2Chr.json records a SAMEKH after that verse — precisely the 29:17|18 seam the revision was obliged to defend — and it cites neither 29:13 nor 29:14, which also carry SAMEKHs inside the span. Marks are weak in Writings and are never counterevidence by absence, but these three are present, span-internal, and of the same class the row is happy to invoke at its edges.
challenges.suggested_action: Annotate 29:17's mark where that verse is already cited, add oshb:2Chr.29.13 and oshb:2Chr.29.14 with theirs, and state in the rationale why span-internal weak marks do not disturb the unit.

challenges.claim: boundary_evidence_refs carries "oshb:2Chr.3.4 (book-wide פנימה sweep: 3 hits total)". WRITER_BRIEF.md fixes the permitted forms for this array and requires refs only, excluding sweep notes and prose annotations; the mark parenthesis is the single sanctioned exception. The count itself is right — I reproduced 3:4, 29:16 and 29:18 and no others — but it is reported in the wrong place, and the entry was added at repair time.
challenges.suggested_action: Reduce the entry to "oshb:2Chr.3.4" and carry the three-attestation count in boundary_rationale, where sweep results belong.

primary_reviews.rationale: This row holds up under a fresh pass. The Levite-roll opening (29:12), the priestly inner-house purge at 29:16, the dated eight-day completion note at 29:17, and the report-to-the-king close at 29:18-19 are all quoted accurately and organized into a coherent execution-and-report unit. The פנימה rare-verb argument for keeping 18-19 attached rather than splitting off a fresh report scene is the strongest available reading and is now made explicit rather than left implicit.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Three low-severity items converge on one row without unsettling its actual boundary. LF's ellipsis flag at 29:15 checks out byte-for-byte: 2Chr_oshb.txt runs יְהוָָד directly into לְטַהֵ֖ר with nothing elided, so the citation's ellipsis is spurious. OL's two items are documentation gaps, not boundary defects. primary_reviews.rationale: Every Hebrew citation here is sound — two drawn from 30:13, then 30:14, 30:15, 30:16, and two from 30:17, each reproducing the pointed source exactly and sitting in the verse named. The far edge is not, and the Hebrew shows why: the row contrasts 30:17's 'procedural mechanics' with 'the causal clause of 30:18', but 30:17 is itself a causal clause and the row's quotation begins after its opening. In full, 30:17 is כִּי רַבַּ֥ת בַּקָּהָ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹא הִתְקַדָּ֑שׁוּ … and 30:18 is כִּ֣י מַרְבִּ֣ית הָעָ֡ם רַ֠בַּת … לֹ֣א הִטֶּהָ֔רוּ; a verse-initial scan of 30:10-21 finds כי at exactly these two positions and nowhere else in the neighbourhood. The two are coordinate explanations of one purity failure, sharing the רבת quantifier and a negated purification verb, so the register does not turn where the row cuts. A defensible seam may still lie at 30:18b, where כִּי֩ הִתְפַּלֵּ֨ל יְחִזְקִיָּ֤הוּ עֲלֵיהֶם֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר opens the intercession, but that is a different cut from the one argued.

The row's quotation of 30:17 silently starts after that כי, which is what makes the contrast look clean.

primary_reviews.rationale: The repair did more than the minimum: it restored the elided particle, conceded that 30:17 and 30:18 both open causally, and replaced the old procedural-to-causal story with a backward/forward asymmetry between the two clauses. Six Hebrew runs are byte-exact and five WEB slices verbatim, including a correctly paired ellipsis on both halves of the 30:13 citation. But the asymmetry itself fails on its backward term. 30:15 reports a slaughter with an unnamed plural subject and then names the priests and Levites separately as those who were ashamed and sanctified themselves, and 30:16 places the Levites at the blood relay rather than at the knife. A Levitical slaughter is therefore not something 14-16 has already narrated: 30:17 introduces it, exactly as 30:18 introduces the eating violation.

challenges.claim: The far edge now rests on the claim that "30:17 explains, backward, why the Levites performed a slaughter already narrated in 14-16", and 14-16 narrates no Levitical slaughter. 30:15's וַיִּשְׁחֲט֣וּ הַפֶּ֔סַח has no stated subject, and the same verse then distinguishes וְהַכֹּהֲנִ֨ים וְהַלְוִיִּ֤ם from that action as the ones who נִכְלְמוּ֙ וַיִּֽתְקַדְּשׁ֔וּ; 30:16 assigns the Levites the blood-relay role, the priests sprinkling מִיַּ֖ד הַלְוִיִּֽם. So the Levitical slaughter of 30:17 is new information, formally parallel to the eating violation the row assigns to 30:18, and the backward/forward asymmetry that justifies cutting between the two causal clauses loses its backward term. Since that distinction entered with the repair, the seam is at present defended by an argument the text does not license.
challenges.suggested_action: Either establish from the text that the unnamed slaughterers of 30:15 are the Levites, or rest the 17|18 seam elsewhere — the prayer frame arriving inside 30:18 is the obvious candidate — and describe 30:17 as introducing the Levitical accommodation rather than explaining an act already told.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the cluster's cleanest unit: the opening echoes 30:2's counsel-verb deliberately, and the close (prayer ascending to heaven) is as strong a completion-style formula as the book offers outside the explicit שלם vocabulary. The four intervening beats (provisioning, general rejoicing, the Solomon comparison, the benediction) read as one continuous causal chain rather than stacked scenes - the provisioning explains the celebration's scale, the Solomon line measures its size, and the benediction is the culminating cultic response to it - so 'high' confidence is earned rather than assumed.

Two of the four (30:24, 30:26) lie inside the span, so a reader working from the refs alone would take the tier-3 data to point uniquely at the far edge when in fact it is spread across the whole five-verse block. primary_reviews.rationale: The three Hebrew runs verify byte-exact (31:2, the elided verb-plus-complement of 31:4, and the opening of 31:5), and both WEB fragments reproduce the witness. I judge the span itself defensible, but not on the grammar the row asserts. 31:3 is a verbless clause - וּמְנָת֩ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ מִן רְכוּשׁ֜וֹ לָעֹל֗וֹת ... כַּכָּת֖וּב בְּתוֹרַ֥ת יְהוָֽה - whose grammatical subject is the king's portion, with Hezekiah present only inside a construct chain; WEB has to supply 'He also appointed' because the Hebrew offers no verb there at all. Two warrants the text does supply go unused. The null subject of v4's וַיֹּ֤אמֶר must be recovered from v2's וַיַּעֲמֵ֣ד יְחִזְקִיָּ֡הוּ across that verbless middle verse, which chains the three together; and vv2-4 all close on the divine name, with v3 and v4 ending in the byte-identical pair בְּתוֹרַ֥ת יְהוָֽה (v2 closes בְּשַׁעֲרֵ֖י מַחֲנ֥וֹת יְהוָֽה) - the only adjacent occurrence of that collocation in the book, whose sole other instance is 35:26. The chain breaks at v5, which ends הֵבִֽיאוּ. The far edge is confirmed syntactically as well: וְכִפְרֹ֣ץ is kaf plus infinitive construct, temporal rather than causal, and one of only two such openers in the chapter.

challenges.claim: The row's sole cohesion warrant - three consecutive royal ordinances sharing Hezekiah as fixed subject, all three legislative acts by the king - is false of 31:3, which is verbless: וּמְנָת֩ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ מִן רְכוּשׁ֜וֹ לָעֹל֗וֹת ... כַּכָּת֖וּב בְּתוֹרַ֥ת יְהוָֽה has no finite verb and no Hezekiah subject, only the genitive inside the king's-portion phrase, which is why WEB supplies a verb of its own.
challenges.suggested_action: Swap in the warrants the Hebrew actually carries: the null-subject continuity of וַיֹּ֤אמֶר back to וַיַּעֲמֵ֣ד יְחִזְקִיָּ֡הוּ across the nominal v3, and the clause-final chain בְּשַׁעֲרֵ֖י מַחֲנ֥וֹת יְהוָֽה / כַּכָּת֖וּב בְּתוֹרַ֥ת יְהוָֽה / בְּתוֹרַ֥ת יְהוָֽה spanning vv2-4 and broken at v5's הֵבִֽיאוּ; mirror oshb:2Chr.35.26 into the refs if the rarity of that collocation is argued.

primary_reviews.rationale: The v4/v5 hinge (וְכִפְרֹץ הַדָּבָר) is a genuine protasis-apodosis construction - one of the tier-1 classes the m8-mesh-r2 contract names outright - turning royal legislation into narrated compliance in the next row. That is a stronger boundary signal than the 'medium_low' label suggests, and Hezekiah stays the unbroken grammatical subject across all three verses grouped here, so the internal unity claim is sound.

The structural repair is correct and checkable. 31:3 is indeed verbless — כַּכָּתוּב is a participle inside a comparative phrase, not a finite form — and 31:4's וַיֹּאמֶר carries no expressed subject, so the referent does have to be recovered from v2. The rarity claim is also right on its own terms: a consonantal sweep of 2Chr returns בתורת יהוה clause-final in exactly three verses, 31:3, 31:4 and 35:26, so "recurs just once more, at 35:26" is exact. The parenthetical attached to that claim is what fails. Calling תורַת מֹשֶׁה "the more common variant" inverts the book's actual distribution, and the strategy requires exclusivity claims of this kind to be grepped before they are written. A second, smaller point: a SAMEKH falls after 31:2, inside this three-verse span and at the very join the row has to argue across, and it is neither disclosed nor annotated on the ref the row cites.

challenges.claim: The repair introduced an untested comparative. The rationale describes בְּתוֹרַת יְהוָה as rare "(not the more common 'law of Moses' variant)", but 2Chr's own distribution runs the other way: תורת יהוה stands in six verses (12:1, 17:9, 31:3, 31:4, 34:14, 35:26) against תורת משה in two (23:18 בְּתוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה, 30:16 כְּתוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה). Restricted to the bound בְּ- form the row is actually comparing, the tally is three against one. The genuine finding — clause-final בְּתוֹרַת יְהוָה in only 31:3, 31:4 and 35:26 — is unaffected, but it is now propped on a false aside in a row whose whole point is that the collocation is distinctive.
challenges.suggested_action: Strike the "more common 'law of Moses'" parenthesis, or replace it with the verified figures (six תורת יהוה verses against two תורת משה verses) and rest the rarity claim on clause-final position alone, mirroring oshb:2Chr.23.18 and oshb:2Chr.30.16 into the refs if the comparison is kept.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both Hebrew runs verify, and so do the counts: v13 lists ten names before פְּקִידִ֗ים, and v15 lists six. The far edge is in fact better supported than the row argues. The register's spine is the hithpael registration chain - הִתְיַחְשָׂ֣ם at v16, הִתְיַחֵ֤שׂ at v17, וּלְהִתְיַחֵ֗שׂ at v18, הִתְיַחֵ֖שׂ at v19 - which accounts for every occurrence of that root in this half of the book (the only other is 12:15) and stops at v19, exactly where the span closes; v20 has no member of it. challenges.claim: Two register descriptions do not match the Hebrew. 'Priests and Levites from twenty' mis-attaches the age qualifier: וְאֵ֨ת הִתְיַחֵ֤שׂ הַכֹּהֲנִים֙ לְבֵ֣ית אֲבוֹתֵיהֶ֔ם וְהַ֨לְוִיִּ֔ם מִבֶּ֛ן עֶשְׂרִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה וּלְמָ֑עְלָה qualifies the priests by their fathers' houses and only the Levites by age, as WEB also renders it. And the six men of v15 are not called priests - they stand וְעַל יָד֡וֹ, under the Levite gatekeeper of v14, and are stationed בְּעָרֵ֥י הַכֹּהֲנִ֖ים.
challenges.suggested_action: Correct both descriptions. The span is not contested; if a positive far-edge warrant is wanted, the registration chain running vv16-19 and terminating at v19 is available and mirrors cleanly into the refs.

primary_reviews.rationale: This span matches the book strategy's own instruction verbatim - 'register-like tithe lists 31:11-19 keep coarse' (book_strategy_draft.md line 111) - so the coarse-granularity call is authorized campaign policy applied correctly, not a bare editorial preference the row invented. The v11 opening command and the v20 pivot into evaluative language are both real, clean device shifts bracketing genuine list-format material.

The repaired descriptions match the Hebrew. וְאֵת הִתְיַחֵשׂ הַכֹּהֲנִים לְבֵית אֲבוֹתֵיהֶם qualifies the priests by ancestral house and only וְהַלְוִיִּם by age, and v15's וְעַל יָדוֹ does subordinate the six to the gatekeeper of v14. The counts hold too: ten names in v13, six in v15, Conaniah and Shimei in v12. The strategy citation is exact — §5 directs "register-like tithe lists 31:11-19 keep coarse", matching this span verse for verse — and v20's evaluative clause is a clean break from list format. What the revision left behind is a third participant-role slip of the same kind it fixed twice. In v19 the sons of Aaron are the beneficiaries, marked by the lamed of וְלִבְנֵי אַהֲרֹן, while the distributing is done by a separate group the verse introduces, אֲנָשִׁים אֲשֶׁר נִקְּבוּ בְּשֵׁמוֹת. The row's phrasing makes the sons of Aaron the agents and drops the designated men entirely.

challenges.claim: The v19 summary inverts the verse's participant roles. וְלִבְנֵי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֲנִים ... אֲנָשִׁים אֲשֶׁר נִקְּבוּ בְּשֵׁמוֹת לָתֵת מָנוֹת puts the sons of Aaron in the lamed phrase as those provided for, and introduces a distinct group of men designated by name as the ones giving out portions — as WEB also renders it. The row reads "the sons of Aaron distributed by name in every city", which makes the beneficiaries the agents and loses the designated distributors the verse actually adds. This is the same class of role/attachment error the round-one challenge corrected at vv15 and 17, reappearing one verse later in the repaired text.
challenges.suggested_action: Restate v19 so the named men are the distributors and the sons of Aaron in their pasture-land cities are the recipients, then let the closing clause וּלְכָל הִתְיַחֵשׂ בַּלְוִיִּם carry the far edge as the registration chain's terminus.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: OL-M8-2Chr-135-1 correctly names two misdescriptions inside an otherwise well-defended coarse-register span. V15's six names are introduced standing ועל ידו under v14's Levite gatekeeper Kore and stationed בערי הכהנים; neither the Hebrew nor WEB calls them priests, so the row's 'six named priests' overstates their office. Neither correction touches the span's edges or the coarse-treatment call, which book_strategy_draft.md's own §1 instruction for 31:11-19 continues to authorize untouched.

primary_reviews.rationale: All three Hebrew runs verify byte-exact and both WEB fragments reproduce the witness. The row's two characterisations survive sweeping. The opening verdict is a real in-book royal-evaluation formula: וַיַּ֨עַשׂ הַטּ֤וֹב וְהַיָּשָׁר֙ וְהָ֣אֱמֶ֔ת לִפְנֵ֖י יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהָֽיו at 31:20 answers the Asa notice וַיַּ֤עַשׂ אָסָא֙ הַטּ֣וֹב וְהַיָּשָׁ֔ר בְּעֵינֵ֖י יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהָֽיו (MT 14:1 = WEB 14:2, offset zone B, dual-cited), the same verb and the same pair of evaluative substantives, with וְהָ֣אֱמֶ֔ת added and a different preposition before the divine name. The success close is stock as claimed - the root tsade-lamed-het stands in eleven verses of 2Chr, and 32:30 וַיַּצְלַ֥ח יְחִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ בְּכָֽל מַעֲשֵֽׂהוּ pairs that lexeme with the same 'in all his work' frame and the same king as בְּכָל לְבָב֥וֹ עָשָׂ֖ה וְהִצְלִֽיחַ. The far edge gains support the row does not claim: 32:1 opens אַחֲרֵ֨י הַדְּבָרִ֤ים וְהָאֱמֶת֙ הָאֵ֔לֶּה, retrieving 31:20's וְהָ֣אֱמֶ֔ת as a catchword, and those two verses are the only places the form occurs in the book - which confirms 31:20-21 reads as a closed evaluative unit that the following unit summarises and departs from. Mark handling is correct on type, position and disclosure: pmarks_2Chr.json gives PE at 2Chr.31.21, following the span's final verse. One note filed without challenge: the triad rendering that mixes English with the quoted Hebrew is a literal gloss, not WEB wording ('that which was good, right, and faithful'), and is not labelled as one - the Hebrew is quoted and accurate, so the claim is demonstrated rather than asserted, but the quotation style would be cleaner tightened.

The pivot out of list format into a summarizing verdict is unmistakable in the Hebrew (וַיַּעַשׂ כָּזֹאת replacing the preceding chain of named officials and genealogical clauses), and the row's 'stock Chronicles success-formula' characterization of וְהִצְלִיחַ is not an invented pattern - it is a real recurring closing device in this book.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: No challenge was filed against this row by either primary, and spot-checking confirms why. Both Hebrew quotations (31:20, 31:21) collate byte-exact against 2Chr_oshb.txt, both WEB renderings match 2Chr_web_clean.txt line for line, and the PE at 2Chr.31.21 is correctly typed and disclosed as single-witness in pmarks_2Chr.json. The pivot out of list-format into the evaluative triad הטוב והישר והאמת at v20 and the success-formula close בכל לבבו עשה והצליח at v21 are both well-attested devices elsewhere in the book, and OL's sweep tying 31:20's והאמת to the catchword reopening 32:1 (outside this cluster) is unrebutted added corroboration for treating 20-21 as a closed unit. No action needed.

post_resolution_check.notes: PE at 31:21 matches pmarks; the evaluative-triad pivot (good/right/true) reads cleanly as the provisions complex's coda rather than fresh narrative.

primary_reviews.rationale: Every Hebrew run in this row collates byte-exact to the verse it is attributed to, and the opening formula turns out to be rarer than the strategy's phrasing implies: a consonant-only sweep of the whole book returns one hit for the sequence behind “after these things”, namely 32:1 itself, and it stands there in the expanded shape אַחֲרֵ֨י הַדְּבָרִ֤ים וְהָאֱמֶת֙ הָאֵ֔לֶּה, not the bare form §1 anticipated. Quoting what is actually written rather than the predicted form is the correct call. The catchword tie is also stronger than the row concedes: 31:20 has וְהָ֣אֱמֶ֔ת and 32:1 has וְהָאֱמֶת֙, an identical consonantal skeleton, so this is lexical repetition and not merely a shared root. The inset decision at vv7-8 holds on a Masoretic ground the row never invokes — the athnach in v8 sits on מִלְחֲמֹתֵ֑נוּ, placing the verse's own major internal division exactly where Hezekiah stops speaking and leaving וַיִּסָּמְכ֣וּ הָעָ֔ם in the second half; a speech-only row would therefore have to swallow a narrative response clause it cannot frame away. The rival split at v6 on assembly grounds is weaker than it looks, since the same gathering verb has already surfaced inside the mobilization at v4 (וַיִּקָּבְצ֣וּ עַם רָ֔ב), making assembly part of the texture here rather than a seam signal. At the far edge, 32:9 fronts אַ֣חַר זֶ֗ה שָׁ֠לַח, a qatal behind a temporal adverbial and likewise a single-hit phrase in 2Chr, which is a genuine off-line restart. The PE standing after 32:8 (single-witness) corroborates the close and is absent from the row's refs — an unclaimed tier-3 support, not a defect. No offset zone reaches this span, so the single-numbering refs are right as written.

The row's edges hold under direct check. אַחֲרֵ֨י הַדְּבָרִ֤ים וְהָאֱמֶת֙ הָאֵ֔לֶּה בָּ֖א סַנְחֵרִ֣יב מֶֽלֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר stands exactly where claimed and its אֱמֶת root does recur from 31:20's וְהָ֣אֱמֶ֔ת, giving the transition genuine backward-reaching texture rather than a bare seam-marker. v6's וַיְדַבֵּ֥ר...לֵאמֹֽר is a real speech-introducing frame, and v8b's report of the people's response is narration continuing the same beat, not a resumption formula, so the inset rule correctly keeps 7-8 inside the mobilization scene. v9's אַ֣חַר זֶ֗ה שָׁ֠לַח restores Sennacherib as subject and is a clean scene-changing pivot. The strategy's own device matrix names 32:7-8 as a royal-speech candidate, so the rejected alternative engages the right rival.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: No digest item touches this row; spot-checked the full span independently rather than taking the clean bill of health from either primary on faith. A consonant-only sweep for אחרי הדברים returns exactly one hit in the book, 32:1 itself, so the transition formula is genuinely scarce rather than a stock phrase, and its אמת stem collates letter-for-letter against 31:20's וְהָ֣אֱמֶ֔ת, giving the seam real backward pull. Hezekiah's exhortation at 32:7-8 is the book strategy's own named royal-speech specimen (§1: '...32:7-8'), and v8b's report of the people's response continues that beat rather than supplying an isolating resumption formula, so the inset rule correctly folds it in. The bracketing marks corroborate without being invoked as drivers: PE follows 31:21 and again 32:8 (pmarks_2Chr.json), tier-3 support the row leaves uncited but owes nothing. 32:9's fronted אַ֣חַר זֶ֗ה שָׁ֠לַח restores Sennacherib as grammatical subject on an off-line temporal adverbial, a clean pivot. Neither offset zone reaches this span. High confidence is earned entirely on tier-1 grounds; both primaries agree and my own check finds nothing to add.

post_resolution_check.notes: Time-frame opener is exactly what book_strategy_draft.md expects at this seam, and the inset-rule check on the royal speech (vv7-8) correctly finds no closing resumption frame -- but the pmarks PE at 32:8, this row's own far edge, is absent from refs while the next row (138) discloses that identical mark as its near-edge corroboration; an asymmetric disclosure logged as a medium-severity defect.

primary_reviews.rationale: The three quoted runs sit in the verses named and match the source letter for letter. The reading of v16 is sound on its own terms: וְעוֹד֙ דִּבְּר֣וּ עֲבָדָ֔יו puts an additive adverb in front of a qatal, so the clause is off-line commentary prolonging the taunt rather than a fresh narrative move, which is exactly the “extends, not restarts” force the row claims. Marks bracket the span at both ends and nowhere inside it — PE after 32:8 and SAMEKH after 32:19, both single-witness — and neither bracket appears in the row's refs. The “letters” attribution is faithful to §1's own listing at 32:17, and because the row does not argue that inset as a separate row the inset rule's quotation requirement is not triggered. On v18 the Hebrew reads יְהוּדִ֗ית; WEB renders it “in the Jews' language” and the row's “Hebrew-language” is the standard equivalence for that term, so I record no defect there. What I do press is how far a single connective is asked to reach.

challenges.claim: The unity of vv16-19 rests in this row on one connective, v16's וְעוֹד֙ דִּבְּר֣וּ עֲבָדָ֔יו, but that adverb governs only its own clause. v17 then swaps to a 3ms qatal with Sennacherib as subject (וּסְפָרִ֣ים כָּתַ֔ב, object fronted, verb singular) after v16's plural דִּבְּר֣וּ עֲבָדָ֔יו, and v18 changes both addressee and location (וַיִּקְרְא֨וּ בְקוֹל גָּד֜וֹל יְהוּדִ֗ית עַל עַ֤ם יְרוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל הַֽחוֹמָ֔ה — a participant/location shift of the very type §1 lists as tier-1). Those two internal seams are narrated as content but never argued away, so the stated mechanism does not cover the block it is asked to hold together.
challenges.suggested_action: Retain the span but re-base its unity on grounds that actually span vv17-19 — the single unbroken taunt referent shared by vv16, 17 and 19, and the absence anywhere inside the block of an off-line episode-opener of the type the Chronicler uses at 32:9 and 32:24 — and add the bracketing marks after 32:8 and 32:19 (single-witness) to boundary_evidence_refs as tier-3 corroboration.

primary_reviews.rationale: The opening and closing frames check out: אַ֣חַר זֶ֗ה שָׁ֠לַח (v9) and מַעֲשֵׂ֖ה יְדֵ֥י הָאָדָֽם (v19) both stand as quoted, and v16's וְעוֹד֙ דִּבְּר֣וּ עֲבָדָ֔יו genuinely functions as a continuative rather than a scene-restart, so the outer boundary is sound. But the strongest_rejected_alternative tests the wrong rival. The book strategy's own device matrix names 32:17 specifically as a LETTER inset, yet the row argues against isolating '10-15 vs 16-19,' a quote/narration seam, without ever formulating the alternative the strategy actually flags: v17 alone. That candidate is not obviously weak. v17 opens on its own introducing frame, וּסְפָרִ֣ים כָּתַ֔ב...וְלֵֽאמֹ֨ר עָלָ֜יו לֵאמֹ֗ר, and v18 pivots from a written act (he wrote) to a plural spoken one, וַיִּקְרְא֨וּ בְקוֹל גָּד֜וֹל יְהוּדִ֗ית, a genuine participant/medium shift that could satisfy the inset rule's resumption requirement. The row needed to confront this specific candidate, not a substitute.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative tests a quote/narration split (10-15 vs 16-19) rather than the specific letter-inset candidate the book strategy names at 32:17; v17 has its own speech-introducing frame (וּסְפָרִ֣ים כָּתַ֔ב...לֵאמֹ֗ר) and v18 shifts from a singular written act to a plural spoken one (וַיִּקְרְא֨וּ בְקוֹל גָּד֜וֹל), a real participant/medium change that could satisfy the inset rule's resumption requirement.
challenges.suggested_action: Have the row's rejected_alternative directly test isolating v17 as its own letter-inset row against the vv16+18-19 host, quoting both frame edges, before concluding the merge is safe.

primary_reviews.rationale: The two repairs did what was asked, and the descriptive work on the Hebrew is accurate as far as it goes: v16 is plural דִבְּרוּ עֲבָדָיו, v17 is a 3ms qatal with וּסְפָרִים fronted, v18 is a plural public proclamation, and the marks bracket the block exactly where the row says. The trouble is the criterion the repair adopted to neutralise those shifts. Restricting scene-breaking openers to constructions that front an off-line temporal marker is not a rule chapter 32 obeys: 32:32's וְיֶתֶר דִבְרֵי fronts a nominal with no temporal element and closes the reign, and the cluster's own next row treats it as one of the chapter's marked seams. On the broader criterion that row applies, v17's fronted-object qatal falls squarely inside the class this row denies is present. Separately, the rejected alternative's second leg has no textual anchor, and two English renderings in the rationale are set in the same quotation marks the row uses for its one genuine WEB citation, which is the practice the strategy prohibits outright.

challenges.claim: The exclusion criterion the repair installed is falsified inside chapter 32 itself. The row holds the block together on the ground that 32:9's אַחַר זֶה שָׁלַח and 32:24's בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם plus qatal "both front an off-line temporal marker that vv16-19 never supply". But 32:32 breaks the scene with וְיֶתֶר דִבְרֵי יְחִזְקִיָּהוּ, a fronted nominal carrying nothing temporal, and 33:1 opens with a nominal age formula — both listed as marked seams by the adjacent decision on 32:20. Under that wider and better-supported class, v17's וּסְפָרִים כָּתַב, which this row itself describes as a fronted object with a 3ms qatal, is precisely an off-line opener, so the stated criterion does not exclude the one candidate it was written to exclude.
challenges.suggested_action: Either widen the criterion to all off-line fronting and then argue v17 away on other grounds — the shared taunt referent and the absence of any resumption after v17 — or drop the criterion and rest the block's unity on referential continuity alone, making the treatment consistent with how 32:32 and 33:1 are classed elsewhere in this run.

challenges.claim: Two translator renderings are presented in WEB-citation dress. The rationale sets “and yet more his servants spoke…” after וְעוֹד דִבְּרוּ עֲבָדָיו and “letters he wrote” after וּסְפָרִים כָּתַב, in the same curly double quotes it uses for “the work of men's hands”, which is verbatim WEB at 32:19. Neither of the first two is in the witness: 2Chr_web_clean.txt reads "His servants spoke yet more against Yahweh God" at v16 and "He also wrote letters insulting Yahweh" at v17. The strategy is explicit that translator glosses are labelled as such and never presented as WEB text, and the round-one challenge on decision 134 was upheld on this exact point, where the repaired row now labels its glosses correctly.
challenges.suggested_action: Label both as literal renderings, or reset them in the row's gloss typography, so a reader can tell which of the three English strings in that sentence run is a witness citation; alternatively substitute the actual WEB wording for v16 and v17.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative's second leg is not supported by the text. It sets aside the v17 inset partly because "v18's proclamation immediately reports the letters' own content aloud", but 32:18 names no object of speech — וַיִּקְרְאוּ בְקוֹל גָּדוֹל יְהוּדִית עַל עַם יְרוּשָׁלִם states audience, language and purpose only. The letters' content is in fact quoted inside v17 itself, under its own doubled לֵאמֹר frame, which weakens rather than strengthens the case that v18 functions as v17's resumption.
challenges.suggested_action: Drop the claim that v18 voices the letters, and rest the host-integrity argument on what the text does show: no resumption formula anywhere after v17, and one continuous blasphemy referent closed by v19's מַעֲשֵׂה יְדֵי הָאָדָם.

primary_reviews.rationale: All six Hebrew quotations (32:9, 16, 17, 18, 19, plus the comparison seams at 32:1, 32:24) match the MT text exactly. The row's application of the inset rule and the marker policy both track the book strategy document faithfully: the strategy explicitly lists 'Sennacherib's letters notice 32:17' as a letter-inset candidate, and the row correctly finds no isolating frame around it.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: LF and OL converge on the same underlying gap from different angles, and both hold up under my own collation. LF's proposed test would very likely reconfirm the merge rather than overturn it, but the row should still walk through it by name rather than substituting the weaker 10-15/16-19 quote-narration rival it argued instead. Neither challenge disputes the span; both expose the same argumentation shortfall, reconciled here into one remedy: re-ground the unity claim in the shared taunt referent running through vv16-19 and the absence of any off-line opener inside the block, and mirror the bracketing PE (32.8) and SAMEKH (32.19) into boundary_evidence_refs as tier-3 corroboration, which neither witness currently cites.

The in-book distribution runs against the closural function the row asserts.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: This pair is where the two primaries genuinely split, and it is worth saying plainly which side the text supports. LF's supports verdict took the row's 'temporal closure phrase' label for מֵאַֽחֲרֵי כֵֽן at face value; OL's challenge instead ran the phrase family through the book and the two readings are not equally grounded. A sweep for אחרי כן returns exactly five hits: 20:1 (וַיְהִ֣י אַֽחֲרֵי כֵ֡ן followed by a new subject, 'the children of Moab came'), 20:35 (וְאַחֲרֵי כֵ֗ן אֶתְחַבַּ֛ר, new subject Jehoshaphat), 24:4 (וַיְהִ֖י אַחֲרֵי כֵ֑ן, new subject 'it was in Joash's heart'), and 33:14 (וְאַחֲרֵי כֵ֡ן בָּנָ֣ה, new action), all four clause-initial and opening a fresh episode — plus 32:23, the sole instance carrying the prefixed מן and the sole one standing clause-final, adverbial to the already-stated וַיִּנַּשֵּׂ֛א ('he was exalted... from that point on'). That distribution runs the opposite direction from a recognized closure device: everywhere else in the book this phrase opens what follows, while here it modifies what precedes and reaches forward past the episode rather than sealing it. OL's evidence wins this disagreement because it is the only side that actually tested the idiom against its own book-wide distribution rather than accepting the English gloss's closural feel. The second OL item follows from the first plus the 139 finding: grading this row 'high' does not register that its left edge (the 32:20/21 join ruled on above) is the softest boundary in the entire run while its right edge is comparatively firm, an asymmetry a uniform high rating papers over. Both items are supported; neither changes the span, and both flow into the same open question already logged against 139 — whether v20 belongs here as one continuous petition-and-deliverance unit, which the author/boss round should resolve together with 139's tier-1 warrant question rather than in isolation.

primary_reviews.rationale: All three runs match their source lines exactly. The opening signal is a stronger and scarcer datum than the row's wording suggests: בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם occurs precisely once in 2Chr, at 32:24, so calling it the Chronicler's habitual marker overstates its currency — but a unique fronted time-frame phrase sitting at a seam is if anything better boundary evidence than a recurring one, and the construction is off-line qatal, which is what matters. The moral arc is quoted correctly, and the row could have made more of the hinge it half-notices: v25's כִּ֥י גָבַ֖הּ לִבּ֑וֹ is answered in v26 by וַיִּכָּנַ֤ע יְחִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ בְּגֹ֣בַהּ לִבּ֔וֹ, the identical pride-of-heart wording turned inside out, before בִּימֵ֖י יְחִזְקִיָּֽהוּ limits the reprieve to his lifetime. No mark follows 32:26, which under §2 is not counterevidence and I do not treat it as any. The failure is in what the row says lies beyond its right edge.

challenges.claim: The assertion that v27 opens a topic with “no narrative continuity to the illness account” is contradicted by the text inside the row's own field of view. v31 reads לִדְרֹ֗שׁ הַמּוֹפֵת֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיָ֣ה בָאָ֔רֶץ with the article, and that lexeme for a portent occurs exactly twice in the whole of 2Chr on a consonant-only sweep — 32:24 and 32:31 — so the determined הַמּוֹפֵת֙ in v31 can only be anaphoric to the indefinite וּמוֹפֵ֖ת נָ֥תַן לֽוֹ that closes v24, a verse belonging to this row. The material after v26 is therefore explicitly bound back to the illness notice, and the rejected alternative (a vv24-31 block) is dismissed on a ground the Hebrew refutes.
challenges.suggested_action: Keep the 26/27 seam if it can stand on v27's own topic-opening וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיחִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ together with the pride-of-heart closure running across vv25-26, but strike the “no narrative continuity” assertion and rewrite the rejected alternative so that it concedes and answers the portent-anaphora. Mirror oshb:2Chr.32.31 into boundary_evidence_refs, since that comparandum is now in play for this row's right edge.

primary_reviews.rationale: בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם חָלָ֥ה יְחִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ עַד לָמ֑וּת opens a genuinely new, unconnected crisis, and the moral arc it traces, pride, wrath, humbling, closes on בִּימֵ֖י יְחִזְקִיָּֽהוּ before v27's וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיחִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ עֹ֥שֶׁר וְכָב֖וֹד opens the unrelated wealth topic. 'In the days of Hezekiah' isn't one of the strategy's named formula classes, so the closure argument in practice leans more on the topic shift at v27 than on that phrase alone, which is the right emphasis since the topic change is the stronger signal regardless. The rejected alternative honestly engages the strategy's own flagged low-confidence region (32:24-31) rather than dodging it.

The portent repair holds up under checking: a consonant-only sweep puts מופת at 32:24 and 32:31 and at no third place in the book, so the anaphora the row concedes is real and correctly bounded, and the concession is now load-bearing in the rejected alternative rather than decorative. The trouble is what the seam is made to stand on once that concession is absorbed. Of the two warrants offered for keeping 26/27, only the first — v27's own topic-opening וַיְהִי לִיחִזְקִיָּהוּ — is tested against the book. The second is asserted twice and never tested, and it is asserted in terms this cluster's own decision 140 has just spent a paragraph refusing for a structurally identical adjunct. The row's left-edge description also carries over an overstatement of the same shape as the one the cure removed at the right edge. Confidence medium_low is right for a span the book strategy already flags at §6 as a low-confidence region (32:24-31).

challenges.claim: The 26/27 seam is carried in part by a device the row never establishes: בִּימֵי יְחִזְקִיָּהוּ is called a seal in the rationale and a “moral-closure formula” in the rejected alternative, credited twice with sealing vv25-26. In-book distribution does not support formula status. The בימי + name family occurs five times (9:20, 13:20, 26:5 twice, 32:26); 32:26 is the only clause-final instance, and at none of the other four does the phrase close a unit. One clause-final occurrence cannot constitute a device class — which is exactly the test decision 140 applies inside this same cluster when it refuses closural force to מֵאַחֲרֵי כֵן at 32:23, likewise a unique clause-final temporal adjunct. The cluster currently grades one construction class two different ways.
challenges.suggested_action: Drop “formula” and “sealed”, rest the seam on v27's topic-opening clause plus the completed pride-and-humbling arc, and label any retrospective force of בִּימֵי יְחִזְקִיָּהוּ as content inference in the way 140 now labels its own adjunct; or, if the closural claim is to be kept, establish it from distribution, entering oshb:2Chr.9.20, oshb:2Chr.13.20, oshb:2Chr.26.5 as comparanda in the refs array.

challenges.claim: v24 is introduced as “an entirely new crisis unconnected to the Sennacherib affair just closed”, but the opener the row quotes in the same breath, בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם, is demonstrative and requires an antecedent; it stands only here in 2Chr, and the only days available to it are those narrated at vv21-23. The illness is a different crisis, yet the text expressly dates it inside the preceding frame, so “entirely ... unconnected” overshoots in the same manner as the v27 sentence the cure removed.
challenges.suggested_action: Restrict the claim to subject matter — a fresh crisis anchored by an anaphoric time-frame to the days just reported — and let the edge rest on the fronting of that time-frame rather than on any assertion of disconnection.

primary_reviews.rationale: The revision answers the challenge on its own terms: it keeps the 26/27 seam but stops pretending the wealth material is severed from the illness notice, grounding the seam instead in v27's own topic-opening formula and the pride/humbling arc's completion at v25-26. That is an honest, defensible resolution rather than a denial of the counter-evidence.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Another case where LF's supports verdict missed what OL's challenge caught. LF endorsed the row's claim that v27 'opens an unrelated topic with no narrative continuity to the illness account,' reading only as far as the topic-shift at v27 itself. OL traced a lexeme forward instead: הַמּוֹפֵת֙ ('the portent'), definite, in v31's לִדְרֹ֗שׁ הַמּוֹפֵת֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיָ֣ה בָאָ֔רֶץ. A consonant sweep for מופת across the whole book returns exactly two hits, this one and v24's indefinite וּמוֹפֵ֖ת נָ֥תַן לֽוֹ closing the illness notice that belongs to this very row. A definite noun with only one prior indefinite referent in the entire book is textbook anaphora, and it means the Babylonian envoys' visit (v31, inside the next row's span) is explicitly reaching back to name the sign this row reports, not floating free of it. That directly falsifies the blanket 'no narrative continuity' claim as a description of everything past v26, even though v27's own immediate opening, וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיחִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ עֹ֥שֶׁר וְכָב֖וֹד, is fairly read as a fresh topic in its own right. The challenge is supported. It does not by itself require moving any verse: the 26/27 seam can still stand on v27's topic-opening plus the pride/humbling closure running vv25-26, but the rationale overstates its case and the rejected_alternative needs to concede and answer the portent back-reference rather than ignore it. This finding is the mirror image of the לב-echo challenge lodged against 142 over the same verse; both point at v31's genuine double attachment, and the author/boss round should treat them as one open question about where v31 best belongs rather than two unconnected notes.

challenge_responses.response: Confirmed: 32:31's definite הַמּוֹפֵת֙ is anaphoric to v24's own indefinite וּמוֹפֵ֖ת -- a consonant sweep finds this noun at only these two verses in the whole book -- so the material past v26 is not without narrative continuity to the illness account. 'No narrative continuity' is struck; the rejected_alternative now concedes and answers the portent back-reference rather than ignoring it, while the 26/27 seam itself stands on v27's own topic-opening plus the pride/humbling closure of vv25-26.
